performers: National Symphony Orchestra of London, Walter Goehr
intro: Walter Goehr brings Liszt’s Second Hungarian Rhapsody to Kingsway Hall with the National Symphony Orchestra of London in 1945. This opening disc side turns the piano’s calls and replies into an orchestral conversation.

sections.mNote: A softer continuation after the opening phrases

cues.title: The slow opening speaks
cues.text: Liszt begins with the Lassan, the rhapsody’s slow half. Grave phrases stand beside capricious little turns, long before the fast dance takes over. Goehr has an orchestra to shape these changes of character, where Liszt’s original has one pianist.
cues.evidence: The Lassan’s contrasting character is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2. The recording source identifies the orchestral performers but leaves the arranger unidentified: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PDP-CH_-_National_Symphony_Orchestra_of_London,_Walter_Goehr_-_Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2_in_C-sharp_minor,_S_244-2_-_Liszt_-_Decca-k1321-ar9230.flac.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Schoenberg’s pupil in London
cues.text: Goehr studies with Schoenberg in Berlin and works for Berlin Radio. Forced as a Jewish musician to seek work outside Germany, he moves to London to conduct for His Master’s Voice. His record labels sometimes call him George Walter.
cues.evidence: Goehr’s Berlin studies, emigration, recording work and alternative label names are documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Goehr.

cues.title: Liszt writes down a tune
cues.text: The rhapsody’s opening melody appears in Liszt’s sketchbook in 1846, noted down after he hears it played. He publishes the piano work in 1851. Later, working with Franz Doppler, he makes an orchestral version in D minor.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard discusses the 1846 sketchbook, 1851 publication and Liszt–Doppler orchestral version: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9. Goehr’s orchestration is unidentified, so the historical arrangement is not assigned to this recording.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: He could fit an orchestra under ten fingers, then end a lifetime at the piano with a few notes left hanging in the air.
facts: Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri in Vienna; Anton Reicha in Paris
Free masterclasses; founding president of the Budapest music academy, 1875
Piano works and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; symphonies, concertos and sacred music
composer.background:
Writing from Albano in June 1839, Liszt told Princess Cristina Belgiojoso about the concerts he had been giving alone in Rome. No singer came on between his pieces; no other soloist shared the bill. He played his transcription of the William Tell Overture, fantasies on opera tunes, studies and improvisations. Between numbers he talked to the audience. “The concert is me,” he joked. A single pianist had taken possession of an entire evening.

His father Adam had begun the piano lessons in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where he worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained Liszt’s homeland, though German and French were the languages he used most easily. The family went to Vienna in 1822. Carl Czerny, a former pupil of Beethoven, taught him piano; Antonio Salieri taught him composition. Paris followed in 1823, but its Conservatoire refused to admit a foreigner. Private lessons, including work with Anton Reicha, continued his education.
